name: GLM-5.2 + OpenCode — frontier coding agent on your own six GPUs
description: A coding agent, not a chat window. OpenCode runs in this container with the repository, the terminal and the file tree in front of it, and GLM-5.2 on the six GPUs next to it does the thinking. Open the service URL, sign in, and give it work: it reads files, greps, edits, runs commands and shows you the diff before you keep it. Nothing to install locally and no third party sees the code or the conversation. GLM-5.2 is a 744-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only about 40 billion parameters per token, which is how a model this large answers at a usable speed: 62.1 on SWE-bench Pro and 81.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, the strongest openly published coding scores available, with a 262K-token context here that swallows a large repository in one session. Thinking is on by default and tool calling is wired up with vLLM's glm47 parser and the glm45 reasoning parser, which is the part an agent actually depends on — without them the model's tool calls arrive buried in prose and OpenCode cannot act on a single one. HOW IT IS PUT TOGETHER: one container, one payment. vLLM serves the model on 127.0.0.1 only — the raw OpenAI-compatible API is never published, so there is no unauthenticated endpoint to find — and OpenCode's own server is the single exposed port. OpenCode is pinned to one release, downloaded to your bucket on first launch and reused after that, and it is configured with vllm as the ONLY provider, so no model in the picker can send your code off this box. It runs on the CPU; all six cards stay with the model. TWO REQUIREMENTS AT LAUNCH, both enforced by the startup script rather than discovered later. First, set OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD (12+ characters). This is not the same kind of login as a chat UI: OpenCode's tools run shell commands and write files in this container, HTTP basic auth is the only access control its server has, and it is off unless the password is set — so an unset password means anyone who finds the URL gets a shell for the rest of the paid window. With it set, every route answers 401 without credentials: the UI, the REST API and the event stream. The username defaults to `opencode` and can be changed with OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME. Second, select a persistent-storage bucket. It holds four things that make relaunching cheap and continuous: the 753 GB of model weights, the OpenCode binary, OpenCode's sessions and message history, and — the one that matters most — /data/outputs/workspace-glm52, the project directory the agent edits. The node builds a fresh container on every launch, so without a bucket the weights re-download inside your paid window and the code the agent wrote is destroyed on stop; the container refuses to start rather than let that happen. Bring code in and take it out through the bucket. Shell commands ask for approval before they run and edits inside the workspace do not; change that, or add MCP servers, project instructions and agents, by dropping an opencode.json or AGENTS.md into the workspace — project config wins over the node-managed global config, which is rewritten on every launch. FIRST LAUNCH IS SLOW AND THAT TIME IS BILLED: the weights are 753 GB and are fetched from Hugging Face before the model can load — roughly one and a half to two hours on a gigabit link, minutes on a fast one. Every launch after that reads them from your bucket. Buy a duration that accounts for it, and keep using the same bucket. The service is not published until the script has sent it one real request and got an answer back, so a container that reports Running can actually answer — pipeline-parallel models allocate memory on the first request that startup cannot see, and discovering that by typing a prompt is how a paid window gets wasted. REQUIREMENTS THIS TEMPLATE WILL NOT COMPROMISE ON, each checked before the download starts so a mistake costs seconds rather than hours: OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD, exactly six GPUs of the 141 GB H200 class (132 GB is the arithmetic floor), a large /dev/shm (the node operator must configure it — see the GPU note below), and around 800 GB free on the bucket. If any is missing the container exits immediately with a log line saying which.
outcome: Open a browser and put a frontier-class 744B coding agent to work on a persistent workspace, with the model running entirely on your own six GPUs — code, sessions and history persist across launches.

workflows.name: Weights, workspace and history bucket
workflows.description: Not a workflow. This entry exists so the launch wizard offers the bucket picker: nodes-dashboard gates that picker on workflows[].length > 0 (templateNeedsBucketPicker in src/services/template-launch.ts). The bucket holds the 753 GB of model weights, the OpenCode binary, OpenCode's session history and the workspace the agent edits — without it the container refuses to start. The graph is deliberately empty and the container ignores COMFY_WORKFLOW entirely. Delete this once the node exposes a declarative persistence field.

requiredResources.description: EXACTLY six CUDA GPUs of at least 132 GB VRAM each — in practice the 141 GB H200 class — on one host, ideally NVLink-connected. Six is not a suggestion and not a minimum you can round up from: the model is 753 GB in FP8 and is split with tensor-parallel size 2 across pipeline-parallel size 3, which is the only layout that fits. Tensor-parallel 6 is arithmetically impossible here (the model has 64 attention heads, which 6 does not divide), and replicating the model per GPU would need 140 GB of a 141 GB card before any cache. At this layout each card holds about 125.5 GB of weights, which is why 132 GB is a floor and not a preference: six 96 GB cards cannot run this and never could, 576 GB of VRAM against 753 GB of weights. vLLM is given 93% of the card rather than everything that fits, because a pipeline-parallel model allocates memory on its FIRST REQUEST that startup never profiles — the per-stage NCCL communicators are created lazily on the first hidden-state send, at roughly 100 MB each, alongside the sparse-prefill workspace and a kernel that JIT-compiles mid-inference. Squeeze that headroom out and the service loads, reports healthy and then dies on the first prompt with an NCCL out-of-memory error. The remaining ~5.6 GB per card is still several hundred thousand tokens of KV cache, because the model's compressed-latent attention costs only about 44 KB per token across all 78 layers, each pipeline stage holds only its own 26, and the cache is fp8 — so the 262K context is nowhere near the limit. Override with VLLM_GPU_MEM_UTIL on cards larger than 141 GB. The launch script proves all of this by serving itself one real request before the service is published, so a bad value costs seconds instead of a paid window. ONE OPERATOR PREREQUISITE: a service spanning several GPUs runs one worker process per card, and those processes exchange data through shared memory, so the node must give this container more than Docker's default 64 MB /dev/shm. The node operator sets this once per GPU resource via init.advanced (ShmSize, optionally IpcMode, PidsLimit) — see docs/compute.md, "Multi-GPU workloads". The launch script checks for it up front and exits with an explanatory log line rather than failing obscurely deep inside model loading. OpenCode is pinned to the CPU on purpose, so nothing competes with the model for VRAM.
